note: Amalfi — one of the four Italian maritime republics (with Venice, Genoa, and Pisa) — was absorbed into the Norman Kingdom of Sicily after Robert Guiscard's conquest of southern Italy. Amalfi had been a nominally Byzantine city-state that built its commercial empire on trade between the Islamic world, Byzantium, and Western Europe; its merchants established trading posts throughout the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. Norman conquest (1073, formalized 1131) ended Amalfi's independent commercial role; Pisa's subsequent sack (1135) destroyed the city as a commercial power. Amalfi's practical contribution — the maritime code Tabula Amalfitana, the compass — outlasted the city-state.

_quarry.structural_significance: Amalfi's absorption ends the southernmost Italian maritime republic; the Norman conquest demonstrates that small city-states dependent on trade cannot survive without military protection; the Tabula Amalfitana (maritime law code) becomes the foundation of Mediterranean maritime law
